front: STEMI is diagnosed at a hospital that cannot do PCI. What is the reperfusion plan?
bottom: Primary PCI is best; if it can't happen within 120 minutes, give fibrinolytics.

bullets.clue: ST elevation; get the ECG within 10 minutes.
bullets.treat: PCI ≤90 min (≤120 if transferred); fibrinolytics if onset <12 h.
bullets.trap: ST depression in V1–V3? Add V7–V9: posterior STEMI.

back: Primary PCI is best; if it can't happen within 120 minutes, give fibrinolytics. Key clue: ST elevation; get the ECG within 10 minutes. First-line: PCI ≤90 min (≤120 if transferred); fibrinolytics if onset <12 h. Exam trap: ST depression in V1–V3? Add V7–V9: posterior STEMI.

diagram.alt: STEMI timeline of ECG within 10 minutes and PCI within 90 or 120 minutes, with a decision between transfer for PCI and fibrinolytics, plus a posterior MI note.

source.guideline: 2025 ACC/AHA/ACEP/NAEMSP/SCAI Guideline for the Management of Patients With Acute Coronary Syndromes
source.recommendation: ECG within 10 min of first medical contact (COR 1). Primary PCI with FMC-to-device ≤90 min, or ≤120 min if transfer is required (COR 1, §5.2.1). If anticipated FMC-to-device >120 min and symptom onset <12 h, fibrinolytics if no contraindication (COR 1, §5.3). Posterior leads V7–V9 when ST depression in V1–V3 suggests posterior MI.

front: Atrial fibrillation: when do you anticoagulate, and with what?
bottom: Anticoagulate when CHA₂DS₂-VASc is ≥2 (men) or ≥3 (women); use a DOAC.

bullets.clue: Irregularly irregular pulse, no P waves.
bullets.treat: DOAC over warfarin. Unstable? Synchronized cardioversion.
bullets.trap: Mechanical valve or moderate–severe mitral stenosis → warfarin.

back: Anticoagulate when CHA₂DS₂-VASc is ≥2 (men) or ≥3 (women); use a DOAC. Key clue: Irregularly irregular pulse, no P waves. First-line: DOAC over warfarin. Unstable? Synchronized cardioversion. Exam trap: Mechanical valve or moderate–severe mitral stenosis → warfarin.
mnemonic: CHA₂DS₂-VASc: CHF, HTN, Age ≥75 (2 pts), DM, Stroke/TIA (2 pts), Vascular disease, Age 65–74, Sex (female).

diagram.alt: CHA2DS2-VASc score chips with points, anticoagulation thresholds, DOAC versus warfarin, rate control, unstable AF, and the 3 weeks before and 4 weeks after cardioversion timeline.

source.guideline: 2023 ACC/AHA/ACCP/HRS Guideline for the Diagnosis and Management of Atrial Fibrillation
source.recommendation: Anticoagulation recommended when annual thromboembolic risk is ≥2% (e.g., CHA₂DS₂-VASc ≥2 men / ≥3 women) (COR 1, LOE A); reasonable at 1–<2% (COR 2a). DOAC recommended over warfarin except moderate–severe rheumatic MS or mechanical valve. Hemodynamically unstable AF: immediate electrical cardioversion. Rate control: beta-blocker or non-dihydropyridine CCB when LVEF >40%. AF ≥48 h: ≥3 weeks anticoagulation or imaging to exclude thrombus before cardioversion; ≥4 weeks after.

front: HFrEF: name the four foundational drug classes (GDMT).
bottom: Four drug classes: ARNI, beta-blocker, MRA, SGLT2 inhibitor.

bullets.clue: Low ejection fraction with heart-failure symptoms.
bullets.treat: Use all four; the SGLT2 inhibitor helps with or without diabetes.
bullets.trap: Never combine an ARNI with an ACE inhibitor (36-hour gap).

back: Four drug classes: ARNI, beta-blocker, MRA, SGLT2 inhibitor. Key clue: Low ejection fraction with heart-failure symptoms. First-line: Use all four; the SGLT2 inhibitor helps with or without diabetes. Exam trap: Never combine an ARNI with an ACE inhibitor (36-hour gap).

diagram.alt: Four HFrEF drug classes with named drugs and conditions, plus the ACE inhibitor and ARNI harm warning with 36-hour washout.

source.guideline: 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA Guideline for the Management of Heart Failure (still the current ACC/AHA HF guideline)
source.recommendation: HFrEF stage C: ARNI (Class 1; ACEi/ARB if ARNI not feasible), evidence-based beta-blocker (Class 1), MRA if eGFR >30 and K <5.0 (Class 1), SGLT2i irrespective of diabetes (Class 1). ARNI must not be given with an ACEi or within 36 h of the last ACEi dose (Class 3: Harm).

front: How is COPD confirmed, and what is the initial inhaler plan?
bottom: Spirometry confirms COPD (FEV1/FVC <0.7); inhalers follow the group.

bullets.clue: Group E = a moderate or severe flare in the past year.
bullets.treat: A: one bronchodilator. B and E: LABA + LAMA.
bullets.trap: Eosinophils ≥300 in group E: consider adding an ICS.

back: Spirometry confirms COPD (FEV1/FVC <0.7); inhalers follow the group. Key clue: Group E = a moderate or severe flare in the past year. First-line: A: one bronchodilator. B and E: LABA + LAMA. Exam trap: Eosinophils ≥300 in group E: consider adding an ICS.

diagram.alt: COPD diagnosis by spirometry and GOLD 2026 groups A, B and E with initial inhaler choices, plus home oxygen criteria.

source.guideline: GOLD 2026 Report (Global Strategy for Prevention, Diagnosis and Management of COPD)
source.recommendation: COPD is diagnosed by post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC <0.7. Group A: single bronchodilator. Group B: LABA+LAMA. Group E: LABA+LAMA; consider adding ICS if eosinophils ≥300 cells/µL (LABA+LAMA+ICS preferred over LABA+ICS). 2026 lowered the Group E threshold to ≥1 moderate exacerbation. LTOT >15 h/day for PaO₂ ≤55 mmHg or SaO₂ ≤88% on two measurements over 3 weeks.

front: Suspected PE: D-dimer or straight to imaging, and what changes if the patient is in shock?
bottom: Pretest probability <50%: D-dimer first. Otherwise go straight to CT angiography.

bullets.clue: Sudden breathlessness or pleuritic chest pain.
bullets.treat: Anticoagulate (DOAC preferred). In shock: thrombolysis if bleeding risk is acceptable.
bullets.trap: Pregnant? Use heparin, not a DOAC.

back: Pretest probability <50%: D-dimer first. Otherwise go straight to CT angiography. Key clue: Sudden breathlessness or pleuritic chest pain. First-line: Anticoagulate (DOAC preferred). In shock: thrombolysis if bleeding risk is acceptable. Exam trap: Pregnant? Use heparin, not a DOAC.

diagram.alt: Pulmonary embolism pathway with pretest probability, D-dimer, CT angiography, DOAC treatment, severity categories A to E and when thrombolysis is used.

source.guideline: 2026 AHA/ACC/ACCP/ACEP/CHEST/SCAI/SHM/SIR/SVM/SVN Guideline for the Evaluation and Management of Acute Pulmonary Embolism in Adults
source.recommendation: Categories A–E. D-dimer when probability is <50%; imaging if D-dimer elevated or probability >50%; CTPA standard test (V/Q if CT cannot be done). PERT assessment for Categories C–E (Class 1, LOE B-NR). DOAC preferred over VKA (not in pregnancy). Category E1–2 with acceptable bleeding risk: systemic thrombolysis + anticoagulation is reasonable (COR 2a). Categories A1–C2: systemic thrombolysis should not be used over anticoagulation alone (COR 3: Harm).

front: Gout: how is it confirmed, how is a flare treated, and what is first-line long-term therapy?
bottom: Needle-shaped crystals confirm gout; treat the flare, then start allopurinol.

bullets.clue: Joint aspirate: negatively birefringent needles.
bullets.treat: Flare: colchicine, NSAID or steroid. Long term: allopurinol to urate <6.
bullets.trap: Start allopurinol low (≤100 mg) with flare prophylaxis for 3–6 months.

back: Needle-shaped crystals confirm gout; treat the flare, then start allopurinol. Key clue: Joint aspirate: negatively birefringent needles. First-line: Flare: colchicine, NSAID or steroid. Long term: allopurinol to urate <6. Exam trap: Start allopurinol low (≤100 mg) with flare prophylaxis for 3–6 months.

diagram.alt: Gout steps: crystal confirmation, flare options, allopurinol dosing and target, and prophylaxis.

source.guideline: 2020 ACR Guideline for the Management of Gout (crystal diagnosis: EULAR 2018 diagnosis update)
source.recommendation: Strong: colchicine, NSAIDs, or glucocorticoids for flares. Strong: allopurinol as preferred first-line ULT, including in CKD stage ≥3; low starting dose (≤100 mg/day, lower in CKD); treat-to-target serum urate <6 mg/dL; concomitant anti-inflammatory prophylaxis for ≥3–6 months when starting ULT. EULAR: demonstrating MSU crystals in synovial fluid or tophus aspirate permits definitive diagnosis.

front: Fall on an outstretched hand, snuffbox tenderness, normal X-ray. What now?
bottom: Snuffbox pain with a normal X-ray is a scaphoid fracture until proven otherwise.

bullets.clue: Fall on an outstretched hand; snuffbox tenderness.
bullets.treat: Thumb spica splint; MRI or CT, or repeat films in 10–14 days.
bullets.trap: Early X-rays miss it; proximal-pole fractures risk nonunion.

back: Snuffbox pain with a normal X-ray is a scaphoid fracture until proven otherwise. Key clue: Fall on an outstretched hand; snuffbox tenderness. First-line: Thumb spica splint; MRI or CT, or repeat films in 10–14 days. Exam trap: Early X-rays miss it; proximal-pole fractures risk nonunion.

diagram.alt: Scaphoid fracture bedside signs, immobilization, appropriate imaging, and distal-to-proximal blood supply bar.

source.guideline: ACR Appropriateness Criteria: Acute Hand and Wrist Trauma (suspected scaphoid fracture, negative/equivocal radiographs); EFORT Open Reviews 2020 scaphoid guideline
source.recommendation: ACR: with negative/equivocal initial radiographs, repeat radiographs at 10–14 days, MRI wrist without contrast, and CT wrist without contrast are Usually Appropriate; ultrasound, contrast MRI, and bone scan are Usually Not Appropriate. EFORT: wrist immobilized in cast/splint until supplementary MRI; clinical signs are snuffbox tenderness, tubercle tenderness, pain on axial thumb compression; proximal pole is supplied only by dorsal-ridge vessels.

front: Treatment-naive H. pylori, clarithromycin susceptibility unknown: what regimen?
bottom: Bismuth quadruple therapy for 14 days.

bullets.clue: Never treated, clarithromycin susceptibility unknown.
bullets.treat: PPI + bismuth + tetracycline + metronidazole.
bullets.trap: Skip clarithromycin unless susceptibility is known; test cure ≥4 weeks later.

back: Bismuth quadruple therapy for 14 days. Key clue: Never treated, clarithromycin susceptibility unknown. First-line: PPI + bismuth + tetracycline + metronidazole. Exam trap: Skip clarithromycin unless susceptibility is known; test cure ≥4 weeks later.

diagram.alt: H. pylori bismuth quadruple therapy drugs and a weeks timeline for therapy, PPI hold and eradication test.

source.guideline: ACG Clinical Guideline: Treatment of Helicobacter pylori Infection
source.recommendation: Treatment-naive patients (susceptibility unknown): optimized bismuth quadruple therapy for 14 days (PPI, bismuth, tetracycline 500 mg QID, metronidazole 500 mg TID–QID); clarithromycin-containing therapy only if susceptibility is documented. Confirm eradication ≥4 weeks after therapy; stop PPI ~2 weeks before testing.

front: Fever, jaundice, RUQ pain: what is the diagnosis and the definitive treatment?
bottom: Acute cholangitis: antibiotics plus biliary drainage (usually ERCP).

bullets.clue: Fever, jaundice, RUQ pain (Charcot triad).
bullets.treat: Fluids, cultures, antibiotics; drain early (moderate) or urgently (severe).
bullets.trap: Add low blood pressure and confusion = Reynolds pentad: severe.

back: Acute cholangitis: antibiotics plus biliary drainage (usually ERCP). Key clue: Fever, jaundice, RUQ pain (Charcot triad). First-line: Fluids, cultures, antibiotics; drain early (moderate) or urgently (severe). Exam trap: Add low blood pressure and confusion = Reynolds pentad: severe.

diagram.alt: Charcot triad, Reynolds pentad and Tokyo severity grades with drainage timing.

source.guideline: Tokyo Guidelines 2018 (TG18): diagnostic criteria/severity grading and initial management/flowchart for acute cholangitis (still current as of 2026)
source.recommendation: Initial treatment with antibiotics and circulatory/respiratory support; mild: drainage if no response; moderate: early endoscopic or percutaneous transhepatic biliary drainage; severe: drainage as soon as possible after the patient is stabilized. Charcot triad is highly specific but has low sensitivity. Grade III = new organ dysfunction (e.g., hypotension needing vasopressors, disturbed consciousness).

front: Severe eye pain, halos, nausea, and a mid-dilated pupil: diagnosis and treatment?
bottom: Acute angle closure: lower eye pressure now, then laser iridotomy.

bullets.clue: Severe eye pain, halos, nausea, mid-dilated pupil.
bullets.treat: Topical beta-blocker, carbonic anhydrase inhibitor, mannitol; then iridotomy.
bullets.trap: Treat the other eye too; avoid dilating drops.

back: Acute angle closure: lower eye pressure now, then laser iridotomy. Key clue: Severe eye pain, halos, nausea, mid-dilated pupil. First-line: Topical beta-blocker, carbonic anhydrase inhibitor, mannitol; then iridotomy. Exam trap: Treat the other eye too; avoid dilating drops.

diagram.alt: Acute angle closure features and three-step treatment, with drugs to avoid.

source.guideline: AAO Primary Angle-Closure Disease Preferred Practice Pattern
source.recommendation: Acute angle closure: eye pain, headache, nausea/vomiting, blurred vision with halos; markedly elevated IOP, corneal edema, mid-dilated pupil. Initial IOP lowering with medications (beta-blockers, carbonic anhydrase inhibitors, parasympathomimetics, hyperosmotics), then laser peripheral iridotomy as soon as safely feasible as preferred definitive treatment; prompt prophylactic LPI of the fellow eye. Medications with anticholinergic/adrenergic or sulfonamide (topiramate) effects can precipitate angle closure.

front: Preeclampsia with severe features: what are the three priorities?
bottom: Three priorities: magnesium, blood-pressure control, delivery.

bullets.clue: Severe-range BP (≥160/110) in pregnancy.
bullets.treat: Magnesium sulfate; treat BP within 30–60 min; deliver at ≥34 weeks.
bullets.trap: Magnesium toxicity: reflexes vanish first; antidote is calcium gluconate.

back: Three priorities: magnesium, blood-pressure control, delivery. Key clue: Severe-range BP (≥160/110) in pregnancy. First-line: Magnesium sulfate; treat BP within 30–60 min; deliver at ≥34 weeks. Exam trap: Magnesium toxicity: reflexes vanish first; antidote is calcium gluconate.

diagram.alt: Preeclampsia with severe features: severe BP range, three priorities, and magnesium toxicity sign and antidote.

source.guideline: ACOG Practice Bulletin No. 222: Gestational Hypertension and Preeclampsia
source.recommendation: BP ≥160 systolic or ≥110 diastolic = severe range (preeclampsia with severe features). Magnesium sulfate recommended for seizure prophylaxis/treatment; continue 24 h after delivery. Acute-onset severe hypertension: treat within 30–60 min; IV labetalol, IV hydralazine, or oral nifedipine are first-line options. Delivery after stabilization at ≥34 0/7 weeks with severe features; at 37 0/7 weeks without. DTRs lost at ~9 mg/dL; calcium gluconate 10% for toxicity.

front: DKA: how is it diagnosed, and what is the treatment sequence?
bottom: Fluids first, check potassium, then IV insulin.

bullets.clue: High glucose (>200), ketones, acidosis (pH <7.3 or HCO₃ <18).
bullets.treat: Insulin 0.1 U/kg/h once potassium is above 3.5.
bullets.trap: On an SGLT2 inhibitor? Glucose can be normal (euglycemic DKA).

back: Fluids first, check potassium, then IV insulin. Key clue: High glucose (>200), ketones, acidosis (pH <7.3 or HCO₃ <18). First-line: Insulin 0.1 U/kg/h once potassium is above 3.5. Exam trap: On an SGLT2 inhibitor? Glucose can be normal (euglycemic DKA).

diagram.alt: DKA diagnostic criteria and four-step treatment sequence with euglycemic DKA warning.

source.guideline: Hyperglycemic Crises in Adults With Diabetes: A Consensus Report (ADA/EASD/JBDS/AACE/DTS)
source.recommendation: DKA: glucose >200 mg/dL (or prior diabetes), BHB ≥3.0 mmol/L (or urine ketones ≥2+), pH <7.30 or HCO₃ <18. Isotonic saline or balanced crystalloid at 500–1,000 mL/h for the first 2–4 h. If K <3.5 mmol/L, replace K and delay insulin until >3.5. Fixed-rate IV insulin 0.1 units/kg/h; add 5–10% dextrose when glucose <250 mg/dL. Resolution: ketones <0.6 mmol/L and pH ≥7.3 or HCO₃ ≥18; overlap SC and IV insulin 1–2 h. ~10% of DKA is euglycemic, mostly SGLT2-inhibitor related.

front: Acute ischemic stroke: what comes first, and which treatments does the 2026 guideline support?
bottom: Glucose and noncontrast CT first; give lysis within 4.5 h if the deficit is disabling.

bullets.clue: Sudden focal deficit; last-known-well time matters.
bullets.treat: Tenecteplase or alteplase; thrombectomy for large-vessel occlusion.
bullets.trap: BP <185/110 before lysis; non-disabling deficit gets DAPT, not lysis.

back: Glucose and noncontrast CT first; give lysis within 4.5 h if the deficit is disabling. Key clue: Sudden focal deficit; last-known-well time matters. First-line: Tenecteplase or alteplase; thrombectomy for large-vessel occlusion. Exam trap: BP <185/110 before lysis; non-disabling deficit gets DAPT, not lysis.

diagram.alt: Stroke imaging, thrombolysis time windows, drug doses, thrombectomy and BP targets.

source.guideline: 2026 Guideline for the Early Management of Patients With Acute Ischemic Stroke (AHA/ASA)
source.recommendation: Tenecteplase or alteplase within 4.5 h of onset/last known well for disabling deficits (tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg, max 25 mg; alteplase 0.9 mg/kg, max 90 mg). Extended-window lysis (4.5–9 h or wake-up) with salvageable tissue on advanced imaging. DAPT rather than lysis for non-disabling deficits. EVT for large-vessel occlusion. BP <185/110 before and <180/105 for 24 h after IVT. Emergent noncontrast CT/MRI to exclude ICH before reperfusion therapy.

front: Alcohol withdrawal: what is the timeline, and what is first-line treatment?
bottom: Benzodiazepines are first-line; give thiamine.

bullets.clue: Tremor starts 6–24 h; seizures 8–48 h; DTs 72–96 h.
bullets.treat: Long-acting benzodiazepine (lorazepam if liver disease) plus thiamine.
bullets.trap: Phenytoin does not prevent or treat withdrawal seizures.

back: Benzodiazepines are first-line; give thiamine. Key clue: Tremor starts 6–24 h; seizures 8–48 h; DTs 72–96 h. First-line: Long-acting benzodiazepine (lorazepam if liver disease) plus thiamine. Exam trap: Phenytoin does not prevent or treat withdrawal seizures.

diagram.alt: Alcohol withdrawal hour-by-hour timeline with benzodiazepine, thiamine and phenytoin warning.

source.guideline: ASAM Clinical Practice Guideline on Alcohol Withdrawal Management
source.recommendation: Withdrawal typically begins 6–24 h after last drink; seizures from 8 h to 48 h (peak ~24 h); hallucinations 12–24 h; withdrawal delirium 72–96 h, usually lasting 2–3 days. Benzodiazepines are first-line (IV.17–IV.18); longer-acting agents preferred (IV.20); with significant liver disease use a benzodiazepine with less hepatic metabolism (IV.21). Thiamine 100 mg IV/IM daily for 3–5 days (V.7). Phenytoin should not be used for withdrawal seizures.

front: Hyperkalemia with ECG changes: what do you give first, and why?
bottom: ECG changes: IV calcium first, then shift potassium, then remove it.

bullets.clue: K >5.5 with peaked T waves, wide QRS or arrhythmia.
bullets.treat: Calcium gluconate 1 g; insulin + glucose; albuterol; binder or dialysis.
bullets.trap: Calcium protects the heart but does not lower K.

back: ECG changes: IV calcium first, then shift potassium, then remove it. Key clue: K >5.5 with peaked T waves, wide QRS or arrhythmia. First-line: Calcium gluconate 1 g; insulin + glucose; albuterol; binder or dialysis. Exam trap: Calcium protects the heart but does not lower K.

diagram.alt: Hyperkalemia ECG changes and four-step ACEP treatment with doses and potassium thresholds.

source.guideline: ACEP Management Algorithm for Adults with Hyperkalemia (K >5.5 mEq/L)
source.recommendation: ECG changes (arrhythmia, prolonged PR/QRS, diminished/wide P, peaked T): calcium gluconate 1 g IV push (or calcium chloride 1 ampule); repeat ECG in 5 min and repeat calcium if changes persist. Shift: regular insulin 5 units (insulin-naive or CKD) or 10 units (not naive) with D50 1–2 amps, repeat point-of-care glucose at 30 min then hourly; albuterol 10 mg nebulized over 15 min. Remove: loop diuretic (when eGFR ≥45), oral binders (sodium zirconium cyclosilicate 10–30 g), hemodialysis. Re-assess after 2–4 h: K <6 consider insulin/dextrose + albuterol ± binders ± furosemide; K 6–6.5 administer insulin/dextrose + albuterol, consider urgent hemodialysis; K >6.5 arrange immediate hemodialysis. Consider bicarbonate for metabolic acidosis. UK Kidney Association 2023 guideline used as a cross-check (UK calcium dose differs).

front: Sudden severe scrotal pain in an adolescent: top diagnosis and next step?
bottom: Testicular torsion is a surgical emergency: operate, don't wait for imaging.

bullets.clue: Sudden severe pain, vomiting, high-riding testis, no cremasteric reflex.
bullets.treat: Urgent exploration and detorsion; fix the other testis too.
bullets.trap: Salvage falls fast: near 100% by 6 h, about 20% after 12 h.

back: Testicular torsion is a surgical emergency: operate, don't wait for imaging. Key clue: Sudden severe pain, vomiting, high-riding testis, no cremasteric reflex. First-line: Urgent exploration and detorsion; fix the other testis too. Exam trap: Salvage falls fast: near 100% by 6 h, about 20% after 12 h.

diagram.alt: TWIST score points and risk bands, testis salvage by hours, and surgical steps.

source.guideline: AUA Medical Student Curriculum: Acute Scrotum (testicular torsion); ACR Appropriateness Criteria: Acute Onset of Scrotal Pain, Without Trauma, Without Antecedent Mass
source.recommendation: With a high degree of clinical suspicion, surgical exploration without delay; imaging should not delay exploration. TWIST score: testicular swelling 2, hard testis 2, absent cremasteric reflex 1, nausea/vomiting 1, high-riding testis 1; 0–2 low risk, 3–4 intermediate (ultrasound warranted), ≥5 high risk. When torsion is diagnosed, urgent surgical exploration and detorsion is mandated. Salvage approaches 100% within 6 h of pain onset, about 20% viability if torsion persists >12 h, virtually none beyond 24 h (guidelines, not guarantees). Contralateral testis is delivered and fixed (orchiopexy). Manual detorsion ("opening the book") is an adjunct, not a replacement. ACR AC 2024 supports Doppler ultrasound when the diagnosis is uncertain. Supplemental: RACS 2022 and AAFP 2022 point-of-care guide.

front: Fever, hemolytic anemia with schistocytes, low platelets, renal and neuro changes: diagnosis and first treatment?
bottom: Draw ADAMTS13, then start plasma exchange plus steroids at once.

bullets.clue: Fever, hemolytic anemia, low platelets, kidney and neuro signs.
bullets.treat: Plasma exchange + corticosteroids; rituximab or caplacizumab as add-ons.
bullets.trap: ADAMTS13 <10% confirms it, but never wait for the result.

back: Draw ADAMTS13, then start plasma exchange plus steroids at once. Key clue: Fever, hemolytic anemia, low platelets, kidney and neuro signs. First-line: Plasma exchange + corticosteroids; rituximab or caplacizumab as add-ons. Exam trap: ADAMTS13 <10% confirms it, but never wait for the result.
mnemonic: FAT RN: Fever, Anemia (hemolytic), Thrombocytopenia, Renal dysfunction, Neurologic changes.

diagram.alt: FAT RN pentad and TTP treatment sequence with ADAMTS13 sampling and add-ons.

source.guideline: ISTH Guidelines for Treatment and for Diagnosis of TTP (2020; treatment recommendations reaffirmed in the 2025 focused update)
source.recommendation: Treatment Rec 1: for first acute iTTP event, add corticosteroids to therapeutic plasma exchange (strong). Conditional: add rituximab; add caplacizumab. Diagnosis Rec 1 (≥90% pretest probability): collect ADAMTS13 sample before TPE or any blood product; start TPE and corticosteroids without waiting for ADAMTS13; ADAMTS13 activity <10 IU/dL is the hallmark of TTP and distinguishes it from HUS. 2025 focused update: no change to iTTP recommendations.

front: Suspected bacterial meningitis in an adult: what is the empiric management?
bottom: Don't delay antibiotics; give dexamethasone with the first dose.

bullets.clue: Fever, headache, stiff neck, confusion.
bullets.treat: Vancomycin + ceftriaxone; add ampicillin if older (Listeria).
bullets.trap: CT before LP only with risk features, such as seizure or focal deficit.

back: Don't delay antibiotics; give dexamethasone with the first dose. Key clue: Fever, headache, stiff neck, confusion. First-line: Vancomycin + ceftriaxone; add ampicillin if older (Listeria). Exam trap: CT before LP only with risk features, such as seizure or focal deficit.

diagram.alt: Meningitis dexamethasone, empiric antibiotics, Listeria age cut-off differences among guidelines, and CT-before-LP indications.

source.guideline: IDSA Practice Guidelines for the Management of Bacterial Meningitis (latest IDSA adult guideline) (still current as of 2026)
source.recommendation: Dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg q6h for 2–4 days, first dose 10–20 min before or at least concomitant with the first antimicrobial dose, in adults with suspected/proven pneumococcal meningitis (A-I); continue only if Gram stain shows gram-positive diplococci or cultures grow S. pneumoniae. Empiric therapy age 2–50: vancomycin + third-generation cephalosporin; age >50: add ampicillin (A-III). CT before LP if immunocompromised, CNS disease, new seizure, papilledema, abnormal consciousness, or focal deficit (B-II).

front: Primary or secondary syphilis: how is it diagnosed and treated?
bottom: Primary or secondary syphilis: one dose of benzathine penicillin G.

bullets.clue: Painless chancre, or diffuse rash with lymph nodes.
bullets.treat: 2.4 million units IM once; diagnose with RPR/VDRL plus a treponemal test.
bullets.trap: Fever within 24 h is Jarisch-Herxheimer, not allergy; never Bicillin C-R.

back: Primary or secondary syphilis: one dose of benzathine penicillin G. Key clue: Painless chancre, or diffuse rash with lymph nodes. First-line: 2.4 million units IM once; diagnose with RPR/VDRL plus a treponemal test. Exam trap: Fever within 24 h is Jarisch-Herxheimer, not allergy; never Bicillin C-R.

diagram.alt: Syphilis stages, diagnosis tests, benzathine penicillin dose, allergy alternative and Jarisch-Herxheimer warning.

source.guideline: CDC Sexually Transmitted Infections Treatment Guidelines, 2021: Syphilis
source.recommendation: Primary/secondary syphilis: benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM in a single dose. Do not use Bicillin C-R. Diagnosis by darkfield/PCR of lesion, or nontreponemal plus treponemal serology. Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction can occur within 24 h of therapy. Penicillin-allergic non-pregnant patients: doxycycline 100 mg BID × 14 days; pregnant patients should be desensitized.

front: Suspicious pigmented lesion: how should it be biopsied, and which pathology result drives management?
bottom: Suspicious mole: narrow excisional biopsy that keeps the full depth.

bullets.clue: ABCDE: asymmetry, border, color, diameter >6 mm, evolving.
bullets.treat: Excise with 1–3 mm margins, deep enough to include the base.
bullets.trap: Breslow depth drives staging; cutting through the base understates it.

back: Suspicious mole: narrow excisional biopsy that keeps the full depth. Key clue: ABCDE: asymmetry, border, color, diameter >6 mm, evolving. First-line: Excise with 1–3 mm margins, deep enough to include the base. Exam trap: Breslow depth drives staging; cutting through the base understates it.
mnemonic: ABCDE: Asymmetry, Border irregularity, Color variation, Diameter >6 mm, Evolving.

diagram.alt: Melanoma ABCDE chips, preferred biopsy, partial biopsy exceptions and Breslow thickness.

source.guideline: AAD Guidelines of Care for the Management of Primary Cutaneous Melanoma
source.recommendation: Preferred biopsy: narrow-margin (1–3 mm clinically negative margins) excisional/complete biopsy, deep enough to avoid transecting the lesion (elliptical, punch, or deep shave/saucerization); partial biopsy in selected situations (e.g., facial/acral/very large lesions); Breslow thickness is a required pathology element (Strength A).
